en: This Kutubiy standing here
Will stand beneath your banner.
He is your good fortune, he is your support,
The warrior bound to your waist.
This Kutubiy standing here
Will gather with you what has been scattered;
In death, he will share your faith.
Your sheep will share one fold;
Your food and fellowship will be shared.
If you are truly a faithful companion,
Kutubiy will stand behind you.”
As he was saying this,
Kutubiy attended and learned the written word.
He was a champion and a warrior;
He knew God's name by heart.
Faith filled his breast.
To be the gray-maned one's companion,
He became a Muslim.
Abandoning his idol,
Kutubiy now came forward,
Upholding the Muslim faith.
From dark faith he became pure;
Befriending Manas,
He became a stranger to the Kalmyk people.
Kutubiy became a source of strength,
Staying beside Manas the lion.
He pledged himself to twelve spiritual guides;
He received learning from the wise.
Upon that path he was called illustrious.
They made camp along the river.
Manas and Kutubiy
Became brothers for the world beyond.
Together they chewed white wheat flour;
Together they grasped the Holy Word.
Taking an oath binding unto death,
Making their promise firm,
Riding steeds and grasping banners,
Performing brave deeds and fighting enemies,
Fully trusting his word,
That Kutubiy standing there
Became a source of strength for him.
His companions were reckoned by the stars:
Forty boys, with Kutubiy at their head,
Were your warrior's companions.
Of the forty households in Altai,
The wise man Akbaltay,
Broad of jaw and wide of tongue,
A great orator who never faltered,
A warrior rich in wisdom,
The Kyrgyz champion Baltay—
The forty Kyrgyz households gathered
And held a splendid feast.
Calling out like a young goose,
His white beard shining,
My elder Baltay began to speak,
Speaking slowly, setting his words firmly:
“When the head of our people died,
When, making sport of us,
The forty Chinese tribes divided us,
One of us went to Eren;
One of us went to Khangay;
One of us went to the Russians,
Unable to find a place to settle;
One of us went to the Kazakhs.
Thus we fell into suffering.
The eight sons of Karakan—
When they brought them all to ruin then,
Humiliating every one,
The Black Kalmyks and the many Manchus,
When they brought them all to ruin,
The youngest of the eight
Escaped like a vanished spirit, they say.
If we follow the handed-down accounts,
If we ask those who know,
Making Ala-Too his homeland,
That poor Ulak Khan is alive, they say.
Hearing with our ears, seeing with our eyes,
Since we came to Altai,
We have not walked out freely.
Of the other kinsmen,
We have heard of none at all.
Have they all been slaughtered and died?
Have they suffered grievous oppression?
Have their heads been trapped in a yoke,
Their heads entangled in calamity?
That they have all suffered humiliation,
That all were sold like livestock,
That they suffered grievous oppression,
That not one of them remained alive,
That all perished and died—
These are the things I fear.
My words to Allah were a lament.
Wealthy Jakyp's brother's son—
There was one called Üsön.
Driving Üsön away,
The Black Kalmyks took him.
On the far side of Beijing,
In the place called Sazangshang,
Among the Black Kalmyk people,
They set him to tending sheep, they say.
They abolished the name Üsön, they say,
And named him Köz Kaman, they say.
He entered the Kalmyk religion, they say.
The idol in the corner by the piled belongings
He calls ‘my God,’ they say.
He became a thorough Kalmyk, they say,
Brought calamity upon his head, they say,
And took a Kalmyk wife, they say.
His wife bore him children,
All his grief was gone, they say,
He named him Kökchököz, they say.
When his wife bore another,
He named him Dörböldöy, they say.
When his wife bore another,
He named him Barbalday, they say.
When his wife bore another,
He gave him a Kalmyk name, they say,
He did away with the Kyrgyz name, they say,
He gave him a Kalmyk name, they say,
Forgetting their kin altogether,
They all became Kalmyks, they say.
I raised a tulpar with ardor,
But driven off, it will not leave the mares;
That kinsman who went far away
Shows us no sign of kinship.
The dark, rugged hills
End in a broken gully;
That kinsman who went to the Kalmyks
Will prove our enemy in the end.
And the trouble is grievous:
Your adversary is Kakanchyn,
Your foe is Bakburchun.
The Flood never struck and scattered it;
Into this very Beijing
Iskender never set his foot;
Of this very Beijing
No one ever demanded an accounting.
The fierce Chinese are a teeming people;
See their multitude—like black insects!
We cannot match them in a clash,
We lack the strength to wrestle them.
My child, Manas, my little foal!
In this land of Beijing
They have broad, dug-out moats;
When their khan sends word,
They have an army that will sweep over us;
They have support to rely upon,
They have a stronghold where they dwell.
My child, Manas, my little foal!
You have proved a hero, proved unruly;
In your valor and your lion's might
You have proved unmatched in this world.
You burned the ground where sedges grew,
You kindled the ground of meadow grass,
You poured blood into clear water;
Told to drink water, you drank poison;
Told to take a hat, you cut off a head;
Told to spill blood, you spilled stomach contents;
You unleashed a terrible fury,
Attacking a people with a royal court,
You left them utterly destroyed.
You ruined whoever you encountered,
You launched deeds monstrous beyond measure.
Esenkan's envoys
You slaughtered once again.
You cut a road through craggy ground,
You attacked so many people;
You stirred up terrible strife.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Those who challenged you, you crushed;
You have left us in dire straits.
You broke a court and took its spoils,
You attacked a mighty people,
You slaughtered their strongest men.
My child, you stirred up strife with China.
You crushed their strongest men,
You made a slaughter of them.
You broke a court and took its spoils,
You made a grievous attack on China.
You drank your fill of blood, grew hardened;
In Beijing under its kakan
You earned the name of bloodthirsty Burut.
Challenging a people of far-flung lands,
You have brought yourself into these costly straits.
If the kakan's people sweep upon us,
They will bring us to our end;
If that deeply rooted people sweeps upon us,
They will slaughter every one of us!
Lord Manas, my little foal,
If we go on like this, these Chinese
Will trample us beneath their feet;
They will scatter our four kinds of livestock,
They will unleash a terrible fury!
We were a Kyrgyz people of forty households;
If these Chinese grow enraged,
They will slaughter every one of us!
My little foal, Manas, hear my words:
If seven wolves attack one sheep,
Will they leave its carcass whole?
If armies march from a mighty land—
We were a Kyrgyz people of forty households—
When they beat us, will they leave a carcass whole?
We came to Altai, driven away,
Wandering, unable to find a way;
We came and kept ourselves alive in Altai.
You have raised a mighty grief;
Of the jacket-wearing Manchus
You slaughtered the strongest men.
What shall we do about this grief?
Raising a din, crying “Kakan!”,
The Chinese will sweep upon us.
We challenged a fearsome people;
Bringing turmoil upon this folk,
They will bring us all to our end.
If dust flies up into the sky,
If an army comes in a throng,
We have no strength to clash with it,
We have no means to fight it,
No forest into which to flee,
No Ogoy upon whom to rely,
No support upon which to depend,
No stronghold where we dwell.
If we face them and do battle,
To bind about our waist as support
I have no renowned Kyrgyz people.
We are a Kyrgyz folk of forty households;
It is stark hell, sheer misery.
We were a Kyrgyz people of forty households,
And amid the seething Chinese
We have been left.
If troops come like black jackdaws,
If they come in numbers, bringing turmoil,
What means shall we devise?
We have challenged the Chinese;
How can we stay in Altai?
Let us scatter our countless livestock,
Let us flee toward the setting sun.
We have come to blows with China;
Why should we stay in Altai?
Instead, my little foal,
Let us go toward the Muslims.
Moving from pasture to pasture is child's play;
Let us think it through and migrate thus.
The seething Chinese—
Let us recognize their might.
Moving on and on without a halt,
Let us migrate to the Kyrgyz.
Let us travel along Ala-Too;
Instead, my little foal,
Let us save our lives.
Let us cut spears from birch;
There are the lost and scattered—
Let us gather them,
Let us bind them about our waist as support!
Standing on this bank and that,
If the many Chinese sweep upon us,
